danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: Natasja og Pierre, der var blevet alene, begyndte også at tale, som kun mand og hustru kan tale, det vil sige med usædvanlig klarhed og hurtighed, idet de forstod og udtrykte hinandens tanker på måder, der stred mod alle logikkens regler, uden forudsætninger, slutninger eller konklusioner, og på en ganske ejendommelig måde. Natasja var så vant til denne form for samtale med sin mand, at det for hende var det sikreste tegn på, at noget var galt imellem dem, hvis Pierre fulgte en logisk tankekæde. Når han begyndte at bevise noget, eller talte argumenterende og roligt, og hun, tilskyndet af hans eksempel, begyndte at gøre det samme, vidste hun, at de var på nippet til et skænderi.

Fra det øjeblik, de var alene, og Natasja kom hen til ham med vidtåbne, lykkelige øjne, hurtigt greb hans hoved og trykkede det mod sit bryst, idet hun sagde: »Nu er du helt min, min! Du slipper ikke!« — fra det øjeblik begyndte denne samtale, i modstrid med alle logikkens love og i modstrid med dem, fordi helt forskellige emner blev drøftet på én og samme tid. Denne samtidige drøftelse af mange emner forhindrede ikke en klar forståelse, men var tværtimod det sikreste tegn på, at de forstod hinanden fuldt ud.

Ligesom i en drøm, hvor alt er usikkert, ulogisk og modstridende undtagen den følelse, der styrer drømmen, således var i denne samtale, der stred mod alle fornuftens love, ordene i sig selv ikke sammenhængende og klare, men kun den følelse, der fremkaldte dem.

Natasja talte til Pierre om sin brors liv og gøren, om hvordan hun havde lidt og savnet livet under hans eget fravær, og om hvordan hun var mere glad for Marja end nogensinde, og hvordan Marja på enhver måde var bedre end hende selv. Idet hun sagde dette, var Natasja oprigtig i sin anerkendelse af Marjas overlegenhed, men samtidig stillede hun ved at sige det et krav til Pierre om, at han alligevel skulle foretrække hende frem for Marja og alle andre kvinder, og at han nu, især efter at have mødt mange kvinder i Petersborg, skulle sige hende det på ny.
Pierre svarede på Natasjas ord og fortalte hende, hvor uudholdeligt det havde været for ham at møde damer ved middage og baller i Petersborg.
»Jeg har helt mistet evnen til at tale med damer,« sagde han. »Det var simpelthen kedeligt. Desuden havde jeg meget travlt.«
Natasja så opmærksomt på ham og fortsatte:
»Marja er så vidunderlig,« sagde hun. »Hvor hun forstår børn! Det er, som om hun ser lige ind i deres sjæl. I går for eksempel var Mitja uartig...«
»Hvor han ligner sin far,« indskød Pierre.
Natasja vidste, hvorfor han nævnte Mitjas lighed med Nikolaj: mindet om sin diskussion med sin svoger var ubehageligt, og han ville vide, hvad Natasja syntes om det.

»Nikolaj har den svaghed aldrig at ville være enig i noget, der ikke er alment accepteret. Men jeg forstår, at du sætter pris på det, der åbner nye veje,« sagde hun og gentog ord, Pierre engang havde brugt.

»Nej, det vigtigste er, at for Nikolaj er idéer og diskussioner en adspredelse — næsten et tidsfordriv,« sagde Pierre. »Han samler for eksempel et bibliotek og har gjort det til en regel ikke at købe en ny bog, før han har læst dem, han allerede har købt — Sismondi og Rousseau og Montesquieu,« tilføjede han med et smil. »Du ved, hvor meget jeg...« begyndte han at mildne det, han havde sagt; men Natasja afbrød ham for at vise, at det var unødvendigt.
»Så du siger, at idéer er en adspredelse for ham...«
»Ja, og for mig er intet andet alvorligt. Hele tiden i Petersborg så jeg alle som i en drøm. Når jeg er optaget af en tanke, er alt andet kun adspredelse.«
»Åh, jeg er så ked af, at jeg ikke var der, da du mødte børnene,« sagde Natasja. »Hvem var mest henrykt? Lisa, ikke sandt?«

»Jo,« svarede Pierre og fortsatte med det, der optog ham. »Nikolaj siger, vi ikke bør tænke. Men jeg kan ikke lade være. Desuden følte jeg, da jeg var i Petersborg (det kan jeg sige til dig), at hele sagen ville falde fra hinanden uden mig — alle trak i sin egen retning. Men det lykkedes mig at forene dem alle; og min idé er så klar og enkel. Du ser, jeg siger ikke, at vi bør modstå dette og hint. Vi kan tage fejl. Hvad jeg siger er: 'Slut jer sammen, I som elsker det rette, og lad der kun være ét banner — den aktive dyds banner.' Fyrst Sergej er en fin fyr og klog.«

Natasja ville ikke have tvivlet på storheden i Pierres idé, men én ting forvirrede hende. »Kan en mand, så vigtig og nødvendig for samfundet, også være min ægtemand? Hvordan gik det til?« Hun ønskede at udtrykke denne tvivl for ham. »Hvem kan nu afgøre, om han virkelig er klogere end alle de andre?« spurgte hun sig selv og lod alle dem passere forbi i tankerne, som Pierre mest respekterede. At dømme efter, hvad han havde sagt, var der ingen, han havde agtet så højt som Platon Karatajev.
»Ved du, hvad jeg tænker på?« spurgte hun. »På Platon Karatajev. Ville han have billiget dig nu, tror du?«
Pierre blev slet ikke overrasket over dette spørgsmål. Han forstod sin hustrus tankevej.
»Platon Karatajev?« gentog han og grundede, tydeligvis oprigtigt forsøgende at forestille sig Karatajevs mening om sagen. »Han ville ikke have forstået det... og dog ville han måske.«
»Jeg elsker dig forfærdeligt!« sagde Natasja pludselig. »Forfærdeligt, forfærdeligt!«

»Nej, han ville ikke have billiget det,« sagde Pierre efter nogen eftertanke. »Det, han ville have billiget, er vores familieliv. Han var altid så ivrig efter at finde anstændighed, lykke og fred i alt, og jeg ville have været stolt af at lade ham se os. Nå — du taler om mit fravær, men du ville ikke tro, hvilken særlig følelse jeg har for dig efter en adskillelse...«
»Ja, det vil jeg tro...« begyndte Natasja.
»Nej, det er ikke det. Jeg holder aldrig op med at elske dig. Og man kan ikke elske mere, men dette er noget særligt... Ja, selvfølgelig —« han sluttede ikke, fordi deres øjne mødtes og sagde resten.

»Sikke noget sludder det er,« udbrød Natasja pludselig, »om hvedebrødsdage, og at den største lykke er i begyndelsen! Tværtimod, nu er det bedst af alt. Bare du ikke rejste! Kan du huske, hvordan vi skændtes? Og det var altid min skyld. Altid min. Og hvad vi skændtes om — jeg husker det ikke engang!«
»Altid om det samme,« sagde Pierre med et smil. »Skinsyg...«
»Sig det ikke! Jeg kan ikke bære det!« udbrød Natasja, og hendes øjne glimtede koldt og hævngerigt. »Så du hende?« tilføjede hun efter en pause.
»Nej, og havde jeg gjort det, ville jeg ikke have genkendt hende.«
De tav et stykke tid.

»Åh, ved du hvad? Mens du talte i arbejdsværelset, betragtede jeg dig,« begyndte Natasja, tydeligvis ivrig efter at fordrive den sky, der var kommet over dem. »Du ligner ham som to dråber vand — drengen.« (Hun mente sin lille søn.) »Åh, det er tid at gå til ham... Mælken er kommet... Men det er synd at forlade dig.«

De tav nogle sekunder. Så vendte de sig pludselig mod hinanden på samme tid og begyndte begge at tale. Pierre begyndte med selvtilfredshed og begejstring, Natasja med et stille, lykkeligt smil. Da de havde afbrudt hinanden, standsede de begge for at lade den anden fortsætte.
»Nej. Hvad sagde du? Fortsæt, fortsæt.«
»Nej, du fortsæt, jeg sagde bare noget vrøvl,« sagde Natasja.

Pierre afsluttede det, han var begyndt på. Det var fortsættelsen af hans selvtilfredse overvejelser over sin succes i Petersborg. I det øjeblik forekom det ham, at han var udvalgt til at give hele det russiske samfund og hele verden en ny retning.
»Jeg ville blot sige, at idéer, der har store resultater, altid er enkle. Hele min idé er, at hvis onde mennesker er forenede og udgør en magt, så må ærlige folk gøre det samme. Så enkelt er det.«
»Ja.«
»Og hvad ville du sige?«
»Jeg? Bare vrøvl.«
»Men sig det alligevel?«

»Åh, ingenting, bare en bagatel,« sagde Natasja, der smilede endnu mere strålende. »Jeg ville bare fortælle dig om Petja: i dag kom ammen for at tage ham fra mig, og han lo, lukkede øjnene og klyngede sig til mig. Jeg er sikker på, han troede, han gemte sig. Forfærdeligt sødt! Nå, nu græder han. Jamen, farvel!« og hun forlod rummet.

Imens brændte der som sædvanlig en lille lampe nede i den unge Nikolaj Bolkonskijs soveværelse. (Drengen var bange for mørket, og de kunne ikke kurere ham for det.) Dessalles sov, støttet af fire puder, og hans romerske næse udsendte lyde af rytmisk snorken. Lille Nikolaj, der netop var vågnet i koldsved, sad oprejst i sengen og stirrede foran sig med vidtåbne øjne. Han var vågnet af en frygtelig drøm. Han havde drømt, at han og onkel Pierre, iført hjelme som dem, der var afbildet i hans Plutark, anførte en kæmpestor hær. Hæren bestod af hvide, skrå linjer, der fyldte luften som de spindelvæv, der flyver rundt om efteråret, og som Dessalles kaldte les fils de la Vierge. Foran dem var Æren, der lignede disse tråde, men var lidt tykkere. Han og Pierre blev båret let og glædeligt af sted, nærmere og nærmere deres mål. Pludselig begyndte trådene, der bar dem, at slappes og blive filtret ind i hinanden, og det blev svært at bevæge sig. Og onkel Nikolaj stod foran dem med streng og truende mine.

»Har du gjort dette?« sagde han og pegede på itubrudte laksegl og fjerpenne. »Jeg elskede dig, men jeg har ordre fra Araktjejev og vil dræbe den første af jer, der bevæger sig fremad.« Lille Nikolaj vendte sig for at se på Pierre, men Pierre var der ikke mere. I hans sted var hans far — fyrst Andrej — og hans far havde hverken skikkelse eller form, men han fandtes, og da lille Nikolaj mærkede ham, blev han svag af kærlighed: han følte sig magtesløs, slap og formløs. Hans far kærtegnede og ynkede ham. Men onkel Nikolaj kom nærmere og nærmere. Rædsel greb den unge Nikolaj, og han vågnede.

»Min far!« tænkte han. (Skønt der var to gode portrætter af fyrst Andrej i huset, forestillede Nikolaj sig ham aldrig i menneskelig skikkelse.) »Min far har været hos mig og kærtegnet mig. Han billigede mig og onkel Pierre. Hvad han end måtte sige mig, vil jeg gøre det. Mucius Scaevola brændte sin hånd. Hvorfor skulle det samme ikke kunne ske for mig? Jeg ved, de vil have mig til at lære. Og jeg vil lære. Men en dag vil jeg være færdig med at lære, og så vil jeg gøre noget. Jeg beder blot Gud om, at der må ske mig noget som det, der skete Plutarks mænd, og jeg vil handle som de gjorde. Jeg vil gøre det endnu bedre. Alle skal kende mig, elske mig og beundre mig!« Og pludselig hulkede hans bryst, og han begyndte at græde.
»Er De syg?« hørte han Dessalles' stemme spørge.
»Nej,« svarede Nikolaj og lagde sig tilbage på puden.

»Han er god og venlig, og jeg holder af ham!« tænkte han om Dessalles. »Men onkel Pierre! Åh, sikke en vidunderlig mand han er! Og min far? Åh, far, far! Ja, jeg vil gøre noget, som selv han ville være tilfreds med...«

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Natasha and Pierre, left alone, also began to talk—the way only a husband and wife can talk, that is, with extraordinary speed and clarity, understanding and expressing each other's thoughts in ways that defy all rules of logic, without premises, deductions, or conclusions, and in a totally unique manner. Natasha was so used to talking with her husband this way that Pierre's following an orderly logical train of thought was for her a sure sign something was wrong between them. When he began proving things, speaking calmly and reasonably, and when she, drawn in by his example, started doing the same, she knew it would lead to a quarrel.

From the moment they were alone together and Natasha came up to him with wide, happy eyes and quickly took his head and pressed it to her chest, saying, "Now you're all mine, mine! You won't escape!"—from that moment, a conversation began that defied all the laws of logic, if only because they talked about many completely different things at the same time. This simultaneous discussion of many topics, far from hindering a clear understanding, was the surest sign that they fully understood each other.

Just as in a dream everything is uncertain, unreasonable, and contradictory except the guiding feeling, so in this conversation—contrary to all laws of reason—the words themselves were not clear or consistent, but only the feeling that guided them.

Natasha told Pierre about her brother's life, about how she had suffered and felt dead inside during Pierre's absence, and how she was fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this, Natasha was genuinely convinced that Mary was better, but in saying so she also demanded that Pierre should prefer her to Mary, and to every other woman, and that now, especially after seeing so many women in Petersburg, he should tell her so again.
Pierre, answering Natasha, told her how intolerable it had been for him to meet ladies at dinners and balls in Petersburg.
"I've completely lost the ability to talk to women," he said. "It was simply boring. Besides, I was very busy."
Natasha looked at him intently and went on:
"Mary is so wonderful," she said. "The way she understands children! It's as if she sees straight into their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitya was being naughty—"
"How much like his father he is," Pierre interjected.
Natasha knew why he mentioned Mitya's resemblance to Nicholas: the memory of his argument with his brother-in-law was unpleasant and he wanted to know what Natasha thought of it.
"Nicholas has the weakness of never agreeing with anything that isn't generally accepted. But I understand that you value what opens up a new path," she said, repeating words Pierre had once used.

"No, the main point is that for Nicholas, ideas and discussions are an amusement—almost a pastime," said Pierre. "He's building a library, for instance, and has made it a rule not to buy a new book until he's read the ones he already has—Sismondi, Rousseau, Montesquieu," he added with a smile. "You know how much I—" he began to soften, but Natasha interrupted, making it clear there was no need for that.
"So you say ideas are just a pastime for him..."
"Yes, and for me nothing else is serious. The whole time I was in Petersburg, I saw everyone as if in a dream. When I'm absorbed by a thought, everything else is just entertainment."
"Oh, I'm so sorry I wasn't there when you met the children," said Natasha. "Which one was most excited? Lisa, I'll bet."

"Yes," Pierre replied, and went on with what was on his mind. "Nicholas says we shouldn't think. But I can't help it. Not to mention that in Petersburg I felt—I can tell you this—the whole thing would have fallen apart without me. Everyone was pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and then my idea is so clear and simple. I'm not saying we should act against this or that. We may be wrong. What I say is: let those who love what's right join hands, and let there be one banner—active virtue. Prince Sergei is a fine man and smart."

Natasha would have had no doubt about the greatness of Pierre's idea, but one thing bothered her. "Can a man so important and necessary to society also be my husband? How did that happen?" She wanted to express this doubt. "Now, who could have decided that he was really so much cleverer than all the rest?" she asked herself, and mentally reviewed all the people Pierre especially respected. Judging by his accounts, there was no one he respected more than Platon Karataev.
"Do you know what I'm thinking about?" she asked. "About Platon Karataev. Would he have approved of you now, do you think?"
Pierre was not at all surprised by this question. He understood his wife's way of thinking.
"Platon Karataev?" he repeated, and thought about it, clearly trying sincerely to imagine Karataev's opinion on the subject. "He wouldn't have understood... yet maybe he would."
"I love you terribly!" Natasha suddenly said. "Terribly, terribly!"

"No, he wouldn't have approved," said Pierre, after reflection. "What he would have approved of is our family life. He always wanted so much to see harmony, happiness, and peace in everything, and I would have been proud to show him our life. There you are—you talk about being apart. But you have no idea what special feeling I have for you after a separation..."
"Yes, and also—" Natasha began.
"No, it's not that. I never stop loving you. And one couldn't love more, but this is something special... Well, of course—" He didn't finish, because their eyes met and said the rest.

"What nonsense it is," Natasha suddenly exclaimed, "about honeymoons, and that the greatest happiness comes at the beginning! On the contrary, now is the best time of all. If only you wouldn't go away! Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And it was always my fault. Always. And what we quarreled about—I don't even remember."
"Always the same thing," Pierre said with a smile. "Jealo—"
"Don't say it! I can't stand it!" Natasha cried, and a cold, vindictive glitter flashed in her eyes. "Did you see her?" she added after a pause.
"No, and if I had I wouldn't have recognized her."
They were silent for a while.

"Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study, I was watching you," Natasha began, clearly wanting to chase away the cloud that had come over them. "You look just like your son—like two peas in a pod," she said, meaning her little boy. "Oh, it's time to go to him... My milk must be coming in... But I feel sorry to leave you."

They were silent for a few seconds. Then suddenly, turning to each other at the same time, they both began to speak. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm, Natasha with a quiet, happy smile. Having interrupted each other, they both stopped to let the other go first.
"No, what were you going to say? Go on, go on."
"No, you go on. I was just talking nonsense," said Natasha.

Pierre finished what he had begun. It was the continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he had been chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society and to the whole world.

"I only wanted to say that ideas with great consequences are always simple. My whole idea is that if evil people are united and working together as a force, then honest people need to do the same. It's as simple as that."
"Yes."
"And what were you going to say?"
"Oh, nothing. Just nonsense."
"No, tell me anyway."

"Oh, it's nothing, just a trifle," said Natasha, smiling even more brightly. "I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today the nurse came to take him from me, and he laughed, shut his eyes, and clung to me—he must have thought he was hiding. He's so sweet! There he is, crying. Well, goodbye!" And she left the room.

Meanwhile, downstairs in young Nicholas Bolkonsky's bedroom, a lamp was burning as usual. (The boy was afraid of the dark and they couldn't cure him of it.) Dessalles lay sleeping, propped up on four pillows, his Roman nose emitting sounds of rhythmic snoring. Young Nicholas, who had just woken up in a cold sweat, sat up in bed with wide-open eyes. He had been woken by a terrible dream. In the dream, he and Uncle Pierre were marching at the head of a huge army, wearing helmets like the ones illustrated in his edition of Plutarch. The army was made of white, slanting lines that filled the air like spiderwebs in autumn—what Dessalles called "the threads of the Virgin Mary." Ahead of them was glory, the same as those threads but somewhat denser. They—he and Pierre—were borne along lightly and joyfully, closer and closer to their goal. Suddenly the threads began to weaken and tangle; it grew heavy. And Uncle Nicholas stood before them in a stern, threatening posture.

"Have you done this?" he said, pointing to some broken sealing wax and pens. "I loved you, but Arakcheyev has given me orders and I will kill the first of you who moves forward." Young Nicholas turned to look at Pierre, but Pierre was no longer there. In his place was his father—Prince Andrew—and his father had no form or shape, but he was there, and seeing him, Nicholas felt the weakness of love: he felt limp, boneless, and formless. His father caressed him and pitied him. But Uncle Nicholas advanced closer and closer. A terrible fear gripped the boy, and he woke up.

"My father!" he thought. (Though there were two good portraits of Prince Andrew in the house, Nicholas never imagined him in human form.) "My father was with me and comforted me. He approved of me and of Uncle Pierre. Whatever Uncle Pierre says, I will do it. Mucius Scaevola burned his hand. But why shouldn't the same things happen in my life? I know people want me to study and I will study. But someday I'll stop studying, and then I'll do it. I ask only one thing of God: that the same thing happens to me as happened to the men in Plutarch. And I will do even better. Everyone will know me, love me, and admire me." And suddenly his chest heaved with sobs and he began to cry.
"Are you ill?" he heard Dessalles's voice ask.
"No," Nicholas answered, and lay back on his pillow.

"He is kind and good, and I'm fond of him!" he thought about Dessalles. "But Uncle Pierre! Oh, what a wonderful man he is! And my father? Oh, Father, Father! Yes, I will do something that even he would be proud of..."
